coordinates.note: The ARIANNA prototype-station paper (arXiv:1005.5193) gives the GPS position of the December 2009 prototype station as 78 deg 44.523' S, 165 deg 02.414' E (minutes with decimals; the PDF text prints 780 44‟ 523” S, 1650 02‟ 414” East), about 110 km south of McMurdo Station; the ARIANNA group's Ross Ice Shelf radar paper (arXiv:1410.7134, Fig. 1) prints the same position as 78º 44.523' S, 165º 2.414' E. It replaces an earlier regional reference point (Minna Bluff, a headland about 40 km away). The point is the prototype station's position; the later 7-8 station Hexagonal Radio Array stations are not individually located in the sources consulted, so it is shown as a campus-grade point, approximate, with a precision of 2 km (both papers are arXiv preprints, so it is not labelled a detector coordinate).
coordinates.quote: The prototype was deployed at GPS coordinates 780 44‟ 523” S, 1650 02‟ 414” East, about 110 kilometers south of McMurdo station). This is about 1 km from the original site coordinates.

depth.note: This is the Ross Ice Shelf thickness at the prototype deployment point, not a detector burial depth (ARIANNA stations sit on/near the ice surface).
depth.quote: The ice shelf thickness was measured to be 572 +/- 6 m at the deployment site.

summary.plain: A patch of the vast floating Ross Ice Shelf in Antarctica, more than half a kilometre thick, where a small array of surface radio antennas once listened for neutrinos.
summary.technical: Moore's Bay station field on the Ross Ice Shelf, Antarctica; ice shelf thickness measured at 572±6 m at the original 2009 prototype deployment point. Coordinates are the GPS position the collaboration published for that prototype station (78°44.523'S, 165°02.414'E); later array stations are not individually located.
